title: Build one annotated bibliography entry
objective: Give a reader a trail back to a source, explain what it says, and show why it earns a place in your research paper.

stages.title: Who said it, and how can I check?
stages.explanation: Your partner asks where that brilliant fact came from. You remember a blue website. The internet contains rather a lot of those. A citation gives the reader a trail to the exact source and credits borrowed words or ideas. In an English paper, the in-text citation points to Works Cited. The annotation after the full entry explains what the source says, why you trust it, and how you could use it.
stages.model: Imagine reading “The walls of Uruk change what Gilgamesh values.” Is that your interpretation or one you borrowed from Ira Spar? A citation lets your reader tell.
modelRows: Without a trail
“Someone online says the walls matter.” A reader cannot tell whose idea it is or check its context.
With a trail
“Ira Spar connects Gilgamesh’s return to Uruk with what a person can leave behind.” Naming Spar points to his full entry, where the reader can find his essay.
Why MLA in English?

English scholars often discuss specific passages and compare editions or translations. MLA (Modern Language Association) gives them a shared way to point from a passage to the exact work they used. Other fields may choose different styles.
Why the same order?

Imagine a class bibliography with thirty entries. If the date moves around, or the website is mistaken for the writer, every entry becomes a new puzzle. A shared order tells readers where to look; it does not mean all sources have the same pieces.

questions.prompt: You paraphrase Spar’s idea in your own words. Why still cite him?
options: Only quotations need citations.
The wording is mine, but the idea is his; readers should be able to check it.
A citation proves his interpretation is correct.
answers: The wording is mine, but the idea is his; readers should be able to check it.
questions.hint: Whose idea shaped the sentence?
questions.explanation: Cite borrowed ideas as well as borrowed words.

alternate.prompt: You describe an interviewer’s discovery in new words. Why credit the interview?
options: The discovery is borrowed, and readers should be able to check it.
Only copied sentences need a source.
answers: The discovery is borrowed, and readers should be able to check it.

questions.prompt: Why does this English class use one MLA pattern?
options: Every source has exactly the same information.
MLA makes sources more credible.
Readers of literature can recognize the parts and locate the edition or passage used.
answers: Readers of literature can recognize the parts and locate the edition or passage used.
questions.hint: Think about the person trying to follow your evidence.
questions.explanation: Consistency makes sources easier to identify, compare and locate.

alternate.prompt: A website names no author. What does consistency mean here?
options: Invent an author to fill the slot.
Use the same order for the elements you actually have.
answers: Use the same order for the elements you actually have.

image.alt: A student follows a red thread from a quotation through author and book to a particular page; a vague card ends in a knot.
image.caption: Follow the thread to the exact page: citation details let a reader check the source. The thread is a metaphor; a citation also credits the creator. AI-generated teaching illustration.

stages.title: Put the pieces in MLA order
stages.explanation: Start with a signed web essay: writer, essay title, website, publication date, direct URL. Think of these as answers to a reader trying to find the work, not five decorations for the bottom of a page. Assemble this common pattern first. Then try a book and notice which pieces change.
stages.model: Signed web essay: author → essay title → website → date → URL. Unsigned translated book: title → translator and editor → publisher → year.
modelRows: Spar, Ira.
The named writer comes first, family name first.
“Gilgamesh.”
Quotation marks identify this particular essay.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art
The italicized website name identifies the container.
1 Apr. 2009 → direct URL
The date identifies when the essay appeared; the link takes the reader to that page.
Source or outside source?
The Beowulf book below is a primary text. Practice citing it here, but it does not count as one of the 2–3 outside sources for your paper.

questions.prompt: Build the MLA entry for Ira Spar’s museum essay.
answers: Spar, Ira. “Gilgamesh.” The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1 Apr. 2009, www.metmuseum.org/essays/gilgamesh.
questions.hint: Begin with the writer, then the essay title. The URL comes last.
questions.explanation: Signed essay: author → essay title → website → date → URL.

alternate.prompt: Practice-only source (invented): Assemble Mira Chen’s web essay about epic endings.
answers: Chen, Mira. “Coming Home.” Epic Reader, 5 May 2024, example.org/coming-home.

questions.prompt: Build the MLA entry for this translated and edited edition of Beowulf. Credit the translators before the editor in this exercise. With no named author, begin with the book title. A book has a publisher rather than a website and URL.
pieces: Translated by Alan Sullivan and Timothy Murphy,
answers: Beowulf. Translated by Alan Sullivan and Timothy Murphy, edited by Sarah Anderson, Pearson, 2004.
questions.hint: With no named author, start with the book title. Keep the publication year last.
questions.explanation: Unsigned book: title → contributors → publisher → year. In the full MLA pattern, use the elements your source has: author, source title, container, other contributors, version, number, publisher, date, location.

alternate.prompt: Practice-only source (invented): Assemble this unsigned translated book; credit the translator before the editor.
answers: Songs of the River. Translated by Lin Yu, edited by Mei Sun, North Bank Press, 2022.

image.alt: Signed web essay: author (who wrote it), essay title (which page), website (where published), date (when), URL (where to find it).
image.caption: Follow a reader’s questions from left to right. The essay title finds the particular work; the website name identifies its container.

stages.title: Say what the source contributes
modelRows: Worked entry · Gilgamesh
Spar, Ira. “Gilgamesh.” The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1 Apr. 2009, www.metmuseum.org/essays/gilgamesh.
Annotation

Spar reads the return to Uruk as a change in the king’s ambition: what he builds can endure even though he cannot. Spar writes for the museum’s Department of Ancient Near Eastern Art and names the translations behind his account. I could compare his reading of the walls with the passage where Gilgamesh returns home.
Your next source
In an On Being interview, Paulo Coelho describes how a pilgrimage helped him choose his spiritual path. He speaks about his own experience; the interview does not analyze the novel’s dialogue.
stages.explanation: “This source is useful because it is very useful.” A sentence has happened; an explanation has not. Replace the circle with a specific job: “I can compare this account of choosing a path with Santiago’s departure.” A summary reports the source’s idea. Credibility explains why to trust it for a particular claim. Usefulness names what you can do with it. A reliable source can still be the wrong tool for your question.
stages.model:
In Krista Tippett's On Being interview “The Alchemy of Pilgrimage,” Paulo Coelho describes a pilgrimage that helped him choose a spiritual life for himself. This is a first-person account of his experience. Imagine asking: How might Santiago's journey in The Alchemist dramatize the difference between following instructions and choosing a path?

Weak: “He is famous, so this is useful.”
Stronger: “Coelho can speak firsthand about his own pilgrimage. I could compare his account of choice with Santiago's decision to leave; I still need evidence from the novel to interpret that scene.”

questions.prompt: Which sentence summarizes an idea from the interview?
options: I plan to use the interview in paragraph two.
Coelho describes pilgrimage as a turning point in how he approached faith.
This interview is credible because Coelho was there.
answers: Coelho describes pilgrimage as a turning point in how he approached faith.
questions.hint: Choose the sentence that tells what the speaker said, rather than your plan or your evaluation.
questions.explanation: A summary names a particular idea in the source. A reason to trust it and a plan for using it do different jobs.

alternate.prompt: In Spar's Gilgamesh essay, which sentence reports the author's idea rather than rating or using the essay?
options: I could use this beside a line from the ending.
The essay names translations I can check.
Spar connects the king's return to what can outlast a human life.
answers: Spar connects the king's return to what can outlast a human life.

rehearsal.prompt: Supply the missing summary. Citation and assessment are already handled: the interview is firsthand evidence about Coelho’s life. In one sentence, summarize what he says about pilgrimage without evaluating him.
rehearsal.sample: Coelho describes his pilgrimage as a turning point in how he chose to live out his faith. Does your sentence report an idea rather than praise the speaker?

questions.prompt: Your question changes to “How does repetition shape the rhythm of Santiago's dialogue?” What should change in your evaluation of the interview?
options: The interview becomes dishonest.
The interview remains credible about Coelho's experience but offers little evidence about sentence rhythm.
The interview still proves the answer because Coelho wrote the novel.
answers: The interview remains credible about Coelho's experience but offers little evidence about sentence rhythm.
questions.hint: Ask what this particular interview actually discusses. Does a new question change the author's experience or the evidence you need?
questions.explanation: For rhythm, you need lines of dialogue and evidence about their language. Author expertise alone cannot supply that evidence.

alternate.prompt: A museum conservator explains how a Beowulf manuscript was repaired. Is that account useful for a question about the poem’s rhythm?
options: Its expertise is relevant to the repairs, but the rhythm question needs evidence about the verse.
Any credible source about Beowulf answers every question about the poem.
answers: Its expertise is relevant to the repairs, but the rhythm question needs evidence about the verse.

rehearsal.prompt: Now supply both assessment moves. Question: How does Santiago learn to choose his own path? Write why Coelho can speak credibly about pilgrimage, then name one specific comparison you could test in the novel.
rehearsal.sample: Coelho experienced the pilgrimage himself. I could compare his choice of a spiritual path with Santiago’s decision to leave home, checking the novel before claiming that their motives match.

final.title: Your turn: Can we date a story from its surviving pages?
final.prompt: Research question: What can the surviving manuscript tell us—and not tell us—about when Beowulf's story was told? Using only the source card, write one full MLA entry, then a 3–4 sentence annotation in your own words. Summarize the source, give a concrete reason to trust it for this question, and explain which evidence you would use and what it cannot prove. Plain text is fine; no special typing is needed for italics. The practice source is provided; for the real assignment, select 2–3 outside sources for your own question on any semester text.
final.source:
Page title: Hwæt! Beowulf online
Website: British Library
Published: 11 February 2013
No individual byline is shown. For an unsigned page, start the entry with the page title.
URL: https://www.bl.uk/stories/blogs/posts/beowulf-online

From the page: “Made around the year 1000” describes the manuscript. The article says some scholars think storytellers had shared the tale for centuries before that copy was made. The library cares for the manuscript and reproduces photographs of its pages. It identifies the opening page as Cotton MS Vitellius A XV, folio 132r. Apart from the short quotation, this card paraphrases the article.
rubric: MLA citation: Identifies the page by title, the British Library website, the publication date (11 Feb. 2013), and the direct URL in recognizable MLA order. Accept MLA title capitalization, straight/curly quotes, optional protocol, and missing italics in plain text. Do not require a personal author or an access date.
Summary: Accurately distinguishes the manuscript's approximate date from the possibility of an older oral tradition; does not treat the copy date as the proven composition date.
Credibility: Gives grounded evidence such as the library's custody of the manuscript, the reproduced pages, or the precise catalogue reference, and explains its significance.
Usefulness: Connects a specific source detail to the question and identifies the limit of what the evidence can establish about earlier storytelling.
final.delayedCheck: When you next work on your bibliography, cover your notes. For a different outside source, reconstruct its MLA entry from the publication details, name its main idea, and explain one reason to trust it and one specific use for your own question.

title: Nested quotes: make evidence part of your argument
objective: Introduce and embed a short quotation, explain its wording, and connect that insight to your thesis.

stages.title: Let borrowed words finish your sentence
stages.explanation: You have found the perfect quotation. You drop it into the paragraph and wait for the reader to applaud. The reader is waiting for a sentence. Give the borrowed words a grammatical home: name the speaker, add a verb, and let a short exact phrase complete your thought. Our fictional student asks for later library hours: “For anyone coming from practice, the clock is a locked gate.”
stages.model: Library access depends on when students can arrive. Asking for later library hours, the speaker calls the clock “a locked gate.” A clock normally measures time. Here it becomes a barrier that keeps athletes out, even if the door itself is open. The council should therefore judge access by whether students can actually get there after practice.
modelRows: Thesis
Library access depends on when students can arrive.
Introduce + embed
Asking for later library hours, the speaker calls the clock “a locked gate.”
“locked gate”
A clock normally measures time. Here it becomes a barrier that keeps athletes out, even if the door itself is open.
Back to the thesis
The council should therefore judge access by whether students can actually get there after practice.

questions.prompt: A runner says, “The hill was a wall.” Keep the runner’s image: The runner describes the hill as “___.” Type just the two missing words.
answers: a wall
questions.hint: Take the two words that name what the hill seemed to be.
questions.explanation: The quoted noun phrase completes the writer’s sentence after as.

alternate.prompt: A commuter says, “That bridge was a lifeline.” Complete the sentence with two exact words: The commuter calls the bridge “___.”
answers: a lifeline

questions.prompt: What made the borrowed phrase fit into your own sentence?
options: My own wording created a grammatical place for the phrase.
I put a period immediately before the phrase.
I used all the words from the source.
answers: My own wording created a grammatical place for the phrase.
questions.hint: Read the sentence aloud without pausing at the quotation marks.
questions.explanation: The lead-in gives context and makes room for the borrowed words.

alternate.prompt: A cook calls salt “a spotlight.” Which lead-in gives the phrase a grammatical role?
options: Explaining how salt sharpens flavor, the cook calls it
The cook spoke. And said a quote.
answers: Explaining how salt sharpens flavor, the cook calls it

rehearsal.prompt: A student editor says, “Our newspaper is a window on the school.” Write your own sentence introducing the editor and embedding “a window” without quoting the whole line.
rehearsal.sample: Explaining why the paper matters, the student editor calls it “a window” on school life. Read yours aloud: does the phrase fit and is its speaker clear?

image.alt: Quotation-mark characters stand outside paper sentence pieces, then fit into their joined seam under a lamp.
image.caption: The joined pieces represent a grammatical sentence; the lamp represents explanation. Quotation marks alone do neither job. AI-generated teaching illustration.

stages.title: Explain one word, then show why it matters
stages.explanation: “The writer uses imagery. This creates an image.” True, but we are still standing where we started. Try: “A locked gate keeps people out, so the clock becomes a barrier for students arriving late.” Now the image has a consequence. Explain one exact word or phrase, then connect that interpretation to the thesis. You will try each move before putting them together.
stages.model: Opposing cuts to a bus route, a resident calls the last bus “a thread.” A thread joins separate things but snaps easily. The image makes a neighborhood’s connection to work sound fragile. If a single route is all that connects workers to their jobs, cutting it would isolate people rather than simply inconvenience them.
modelRows: Context + evidence
Opposing cuts to a bus route, a resident calls the last bus “a thread.”
“thread” → interpretation
A thread joins separate things but snaps easily. The image makes a neighborhood’s connection to work sound fragile.
Interpretation → thesis
If a single route is all that connects workers to their jobs, cutting it would isolate people rather than simply inconvenience them.

questions.prompt: Which detail should your explanation account for?
options: How much the coach paid for the team uniforms
What a hinge can do that a wall cannot
Whether hinges are made of brass
answers: What a hinge can do that a wall cannot
questions.hint: Think about how each object moves.
questions.explanation: The word hinge suggests a turn or a new direction. A wall suggests a stop.

alternate.prompt: A gardener calls a seed “a promise.” Which question helps you interpret that word?
options: What future possibility does promise suggest?
What is the dictionary spelling of seed?
answers: What future possibility does promise suggest?

rehearsal.prompt: Supply only the missing commentary. Lead-in and quote: After a defeat, the coach calls the loss “a hinge.” Thesis link already supplied: The defeat can change the team’s direction rather than end its season. Write the sentence that explains the image between them.
rehearsal.sample: A hinge is where something turns, so the loss becomes a pivot rather than a dead end. A different reading can work if it explains the word.

questions.prompt: Which question tests whether your last sentence has done its job?
options: Did I repeat the quote exactly a second time?
Did I explain why this reading gives the audience a reason to accept my thesis?
Did I use the phrase this proves?
answers: Did I explain why this reading gives the audience a reason to accept my thesis?
questions.hint: Ask what your reader now has a reason to believe.
questions.explanation: A tie-back carries the interpretation to the specific claim at stake.

alternate.prompt: A poet calls a secret “a splinter.” Your interpretation: the hidden object keeps causing pain. Which claim does that reasoning support?
options: Silence can prolong the harm it conceals.
The speaker knows woodworking.
answers: Silence can prolong the harm it conceals.

rehearsal.prompt: Now supply both reasoning moves without a frame. Evidence: Defending the school archive, a librarian calls it “our memory.” Thesis: Discarding the archive would cost the school more than storage space. Write two sentences: interpret one word, then connect your interpretation to the thesis.
rehearsal.sample: “Our” makes remembering a shared act, not one person’s private hobby. Throwing out the archive would take away the records that let different generations tell a common story.

final.title: Your turn: give Dickinson’s words a job
final.prompt: Write one paragraph of 3–5 sentences. Develop this working thesis: Dickinson presents hope as a quiet presence that lives within a person. Introduce the speaker or poetic situation, weave in a short exact phrase, interpret a specific word or image, and show how that detail supports the thesis. You may sharpen the thesis if your reading fits the lines.
final.source: Emily Dickinson, opening of “Hope is the thing with feathers” (254), Academy of American Poets. The speaker describes hope as a bird. Lines 2–3: “That perches in the soul, / And sings the tune without the words,” (slash marks the line break).
rubric: Context: Identifies Dickinson, the speaker, or the poetic situation in a way that prepares the evidence. A brief lead-in suffices.
Integration: Embeds a short accurate phrase from the supplied lines grammatically in the student’s own sentence. Accept plain quotation marks and harmless punctuation differences.
Explanation: Interprets a particular word or image such as perches or the wordless tune; goes beyond paraphrasing. Accept other text-grounded readings.
Thesis connection: Explains how that interpretation supports the working thesis or a defensible refinement. Do not require a separate formulaic closing sentence.
final.delayedCheck: In your next essay, cover your commentary and reread the quotation. Without looking, explain what one word contributes and how it supports your thesis.

title: Making an Argument: Should School Start Later?
objective: Make a defensible claim, support it with evidence, explain the reasoning, and address a fair objection.

stages.title: Give the reader a reason to agree
stages.explanation: It is first period. Your friend has read the same instruction three times. Someone proposes a later bell; someone else asks what happens to the buses. Both deserve an answer. “Start later because later is better” just sends the claim around the room wearing a different hat. Give the council a debatable claim, a concrete detail, and reasoning that explains why the detail matters.

image.alt: An evidence folder and proposal flag are separated by a gap, then connected by a bridge a student can cross.
image.caption: Evidence needs an explained connection to the claim. A drawn bridge shows the job of reasoning, not proof that the reasoning is sound. AI-generated teaching illustration.

modelRows: Model · fictional school
At Willow School, 12 of 20 students at an optional first-period review said their bus arrived before the doors opened.
Claim + reason
Willow should test a later review session because its current timing may discourage students who ride the early bus.
12 of 20 → evidence
These students reported a particular obstacle. The count is more useful than saying mornings are bad.
Waiting outside → reasoning
Even a motivated student pays a cost in waiting time. Removing that cost could make the review easier to attend.
Scope
The survey supports testing a change to this session. It cannot tell us what every student needs.

questions.prompt: Which statement could the school council actually debate?
options: Willow has a first period.
Willow should try a later review session because the current time makes access harder for bus riders.
This paragraph is about mornings.
answers: Willow should try a later review session because the current time makes access harder for bus riders.
questions.hint: Look for a position someone could reasonably challenge.
questions.explanation: A defensible claim makes a specific judgment and gives a reason.

alternate.prompt: Which is a claim about the lunch timetable rather than a topic or a fact?
options: There are two lunch periods.
Lunch schedules.
The school should stagger lunch because a shorter line would leave more time to eat.
answers: The school should stagger lunch because a shorter line would leave more time to eat.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best test a claim about first-period attention?
options: A tally of students staying on task during comparable first-period activities before and after a change.
The school mascot’s popularity.
A count of people who like the idea of starting later.
answers: A tally of students staying on task during comparable first-period activities before and after a change.
questions.hint: What exactly is the proposed benefit: preference or attention?
questions.explanation: Match the observation to what the claim predicts. Liking a change and paying attention are different outcomes.

alternate.prompt: A club says moving practice will increase attendance. What should it compare?
options: The number who attend comparable sessions at each time.
The number who like the new poster.
answers: The number who attend comparable sessions at each time.

rehearsal.prompt: Write one sentence for your principal: should your school start later? Choose yes, no, or a limited trial. Give a reason someone could challenge.
rehearsal.sample: Example: Keep the present start until we know whether buses can also move; otherwise early riders may still have to wake at the same hour. Your position can differ.

stages.model:
Model · fictional school: At Willow School, 12 of 20 students at an optional first-period review said their bus arrived before the doors opened.
Claim + reason: Willow should test a later review session because its current timing may discourage students who ride the early bus.
12 of 20 → evidence: These students reported a particular obstacle. The count is more useful than saying mornings are bad.
Waiting outside → reasoning: Even a motivated student pays a cost in waiting time. Removing that cost could make the review easier to attend.
Scope: The survey supports testing a change to this session. It cannot tell us what every student needs.

stages.title: Build the bridge and answer an objection
stages.explanation: Your fact has reached one bank of the river. Your proposal is on the other. Reasoning builds the bridge: explain what the fact suggests and why that supports the decision. The bridge is a metaphor, not proof that every connection is sound. Test the strongest objection; answer it, narrow the proposal, or change your mind. Evidence is allowed to have limits.
modelRows: Evidence · fictional example
During a two-day 9:00 review trial, 8 of 10 students completed the opening problem; previously 5 of those 10 had completed a similar problem at 8:00.
Interpret the change
More students finished a comparable task. That is consistent with better concentration, but a different problem or teacher could also explain it.
Qualify the claim
Try a longer comparison before permanently changing the review time.

questions.prompt: Which move turns an observation into reasoning?
options: Repeat the number with an exclamation point.
Explain why the observed change would matter for the proposed policy.
Call the evidence obvious.
answers: Explain why the observed change would matter for the proposed policy.
questions.hint: Think about the bridge in the diagram.
questions.explanation: The reader needs your explanation of how a detail bears on the decision.

alternate.prompt: Attendance rose after a choir rehearsal moved. Which sentence supplies the missing reasoning?
options: More singers came.
If fewer singers miss rehearsal, the group can practice harmonies with all parts present.
answers: If fewer singers miss rehearsal, the group can practice harmonies with all parts present.

rehearsal.prompt: Supply only the missing bridge. Claim: test a later bell. Evidence: in a fictional first-period trial, fewer students asked for the opening directions to be repeated. Explain why that observation might matter and what it cannot establish.
rehearsal.sample: Following the first explanation could mean students were ready to focus sooner. Clearer directions could produce the same pattern, so the observation supports a trial rather than a guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which response takes the bus objection seriously?
options: Anyone who disagrees dislikes sleep.
Ignore buses; only the bell matters.
Check whether pickups can move too, since an unchanged early pickup limits the chance for extra sleep.
answers: Check whether pickups can move too, since an unchanged early pickup limits the chance for extra sleep.
questions.hint: Which answer changes or defends the proposal in light of the objection?
questions.explanation: A meaningful qualification names a condition under which the policy would or would not work.

alternate.prompt: A later dismissal might disrupt childcare. Which reply addresses that trade-off?
options: Compare childcare options and their cost before extending a pilot.
Everybody will get used to it.
answers: Compare childcare options and their cost before extending a pilot.

rehearsal.prompt: A teammate worries that a later dismissal would cut practice short. In your own words, acknowledge that concern and defend, modify, or reconsider your claim.
rehearsal.sample: A shorter practice would cost teams preparation time. I would support a pilot only if the school can move practice or protect its length.

stages.model:
Evidence · fictional example: During a two-day 9:00 review trial, 8 of 10 students completed the opening problem; previously 5 of those 10 had completed a similar problem at 8:00.
Interpret the change: More students finished a comparable task. That is consistent with better concentration, but a different problem or teacher could also explain it.
Qualify the claim: Try a longer comparison before permanently changing the review time.

final.title: Advise the school council
final.prompt: Should your school start later so students can be more attentive in class? Write a 4–6 sentence argument to the council. Support, oppose, or qualify the change. Use a specific detail from the source card, explain how far it supports your position, and respond to one reasonable objection. Your position is yours; the quality of the argument is what matters.
final.source:
Research evidence: In a 2018 Seattle study, Dunster and colleagues compared students before and after secondary schools moved the bell from 7:50 to 8:45 a.m. Median sleep duration on school days was 34 minutes longer after the change. This figure measures sleep, not classroom attention; it also does not promise the same result here.

Local decision scenario (fictional): The council can run a four-week pilot, but one shared bus route cannot change its morning pickup during that month. You may use this constraint for either side.
rubric: Claim: Takes a specific defensible position on a later start for this school, including a conditional position if desired.
Evidence: Accurately uses at least one specific source-card detail, distinguishing hypothetical local constraints from real Seattle findings.
Reasoning: Explains why the evidence supports the position in relation to attention; does not represent measured sleep as proof of increased attention.
Counterargument: Fairly considers a relevant objection and responds with reasoning, a limitation, or a practical condition.
final.delayedCheck: At the next class, argue for or against rotating who chooses the film-club screening. Write a claim, supply a concrete example, and underline the sentence that connects them.

title: Advertising 1 · What does the offer actually prove?
objective: Evaluate a line of reasoning and write commentary that connects the wording of an offer to an editorial decision (AP Lang 5.A, 6.A).

stages.title: Read the promise
stages.explanation: The arts team has stories ready and no money to print them. An advertiser offers funding. Relief! Then someone announces, “They pay, so they own our opinions.” That conclusion has sprinted ahead of the contract. Start with the verb: what action has the business actually promised? Funding printing and controlling a review are different powers. The wording must establish which is on offer.
modelRows: “We will cover printing costs.”
Cover commits money to a specific expense. An editor could use that promise to budget for printing.
“They will choose the reviews.”
Choose describes a different action. The offer says nothing about who picks the stories.
stages.model:
“We will cover printing costs.” — Cover commits money to a specific expense. An editor could use that promise to budget for printing.
“They will choose the reviews.” — Choose describes a different action. The offer says nothing about who picks the stories.

questions.prompt: “We will buy the back page.” Which claim follows?
options: The shop can set the headline.
The shop offers to pay for space.
The editor endorses the shop.
answers: The shop offers to pay for space.
questions.hint: What does buy take as its object?
questions.explanation: The purchase is of space. An editorial role would need a separate term.

alternate.prompt: “We will pay the photographer’s travel.” What has been offered?
options: Control of the captions
Money for travel
Approval of each photo
answers: Money for travel

questions.prompt: Which missing detail matters most before claiming the sponsor controls coverage?
options: The number of copies
The cost of ink
Who has final say over stories
answers: Who has final say over stories
questions.hint: Look for authority to make an editorial decision.
questions.explanation: Evidence about approval rights bears directly on control.

alternate.prompt: A bakery buys a banner in a food issue. What would support a claim that it controls reviews?
options: A clause letting it veto reviews
A larger banner
A second payment
answers: A clause letting it veto reviews

rehearsal.prompt: A fictional sponsor offers to “pay for the paper used in the arts issue.” Complete just the missing limit: This funds the materials, but the words do not establish _____.
rehearsal.sample: This funds the materials, but the words do not establish that the sponsor can choose or change the stories.

image.alt: A coin leads to paper and a printing press; a separate path toward an editorial pencil stops at a closed latch.
image.caption: Funding can pay for printing. Control over editing requires separate evidence in the terms; the latch represents that unanswered question. AI-generated teaching illustration.

stages.title: Write the missing reasoning
stages.explanation: “This clause matters because it is important.” The editor has learned that you are concerned, but not why. Replace it with a consequence: “Letting the sponsor approve reviews could block a negative judgment.” Ask: because this exact clause exists, what could happen to the reporting? Distinguish a possible consequence from something the agreement guarantees.
modelRows: Evidence
A cinema asks to see reviews “before publication.”
Reasoning
Advance access gives the cinema time to ask for changes while the review can still be edited.
Decision and limit
Ask why it needs early access. Seeing a draft creates an opportunity to object, but the clause gives no veto.
stages.model:
Evidence — A cinema asks to see reviews “before publication.”
Reasoning — Advance access gives the cinema time to ask for changes while the review can still be edited.
Decision and limit — Ask why it needs early access. Seeing a draft creates an opportunity to object, but the clause gives no veto.

questions.prompt: A theater asks for “advance notice of review dates.” Which interpretation respects the wording?
options: The theater chooses the reviewer.
The theater can prepare for coverage but has no stated right to approve it.
answers: The theater can prepare for coverage but has no stated right to approve it.
questions.hint: Separate information about timing from authority over wording.
questions.explanation: Knowing a date allows preparation. Approval would require an additional term.

alternate.prompt: A gallery requests a copy “after publication.” Which inference fits?
options: It can block publication.
It can see what readers have already seen.
answers: It can see what readers have already seen.

rehearsal.prompt: A printer asks for “a copy of each issue for our window.” The editor would accept. Supply one sentence explaining why that request fits the decision.
rehearsal.sample: Displaying a finished issue can give the paper new readers while leaving decisions about its contents with the editors.

questions.prompt: Which sentence explains why a clause matters to a decision?
options: The sponsor asks to choose the cover photo.
Choosing the cover would let the sponsor decide which performance gets the most attention.
answers: Choosing the cover would let the sponsor decide which performance gets the most attention.
questions.hint: Look for the consequence of the choice.
questions.explanation: The consequence connects an editorial power to what readers will see.

alternate.prompt: Which sentence explains the effect of a right to delay publication?
options: The shop can delay publication.
A delay could keep a critical review out of readers’ hands until ticket sales close.
answers: A delay could keep a critical review out of readers’ hands until ticket sales close.

final.title: Advise the editors
final.source:
Fictional newsroom file
Juniper Music writes, “We will buy an ad in each concert issue. Please send us the paragraph naming our shop before it goes to print so we can check the spelling.” The editors have not agreed to any terms.
final.prompt: In 3–5 sentences recommend accepting, declining, or changing the offer. Use a precise phrase, explain its consequence for the paper, and identify one conclusion the wording cannot establish.
rubric: Decision: Makes a defensible recommendation; accept any position.
Evidence: Accurately uses the specific terms of the music shop offer.
Commentary: Connects the terms to a plausible editorial consequence and distinguishes a request from an established right or outcome.
final.delayedCheck: Next class, a fictional sponsor offers to “share the finished issue with customers.” Without notes, explain one thing that supports and one thing it does not establish.

title: Advertising 2 · Let an objection sharpen your policy
objective: Explain how an objection qualifies a claim and write a policy that responds to it (AP Lang 3.C, 4.C).

stages.title: Find what changed
stages.explanation: The paper finally has money for arts coverage. Then a reader spots a theater ad beside a glowing review of the same theater. The editor says, “Trust us; we are trustworthy.” That asks the reader to lend the very trust in question. A useful objection names a real cost or concern. Find the exact policy words that could address it without losing every benefit of funding.
modelRows: Draft
“Sell ads anywhere in the arts section.”
Reader’s objection
“If the theater’s ad sits beside its five-star review, how will I know the stars were earned?” The concern is the impression created by placement.
Revision
“Sell arts ads on a separate advertising page.” Separate changes where the ad can appear while preserving the sale.
stages.model:
Draft — “Sell ads anywhere in the arts section.”
Reader’s objection — “If the theater’s ad sits beside its five-star review, how will I know the stars were earned?” The concern is the impression created by placement.
Revision — “Sell arts ads on a separate advertising page.” Separate changes where the ad can appear while preserving the sale.

questions.prompt: Which words answer the reader’s placement concern?
options: Sell arts ads
On a separate advertising page
Five-star review
answers: On a separate advertising page
questions.hint: Find the words a layout editor could act on.
questions.explanation: The new location directly addresses the side-by-side impression.

alternate.prompt: A critic wants free review tickets disclosed. Which addition answers that concern?
options: Use experienced reviewers.
Name the ticket provider beneath the review.
answers: Name the ticket provider beneath the review.

questions.prompt: Which objection is the strongest reason to revisit a blanket ban on arts ads?
options: Ads sometimes use bright colors.
Without ad income, the print budget covers only one of three planned issues.
answers: Without ad income, the print budget covers only one of three planned issues.
questions.hint: Which consequence bears directly on keeping the paper in print?
questions.explanation: The budget creates a concrete cost for readers and performers.

alternate.prompt: Which objection directly challenges a policy requiring full-page ads?
options: Some ads use photos.
Small clubs can afford only a quarter page.
answers: Small clubs can afford only a quarter page.

rehearsal.prompt: A draft rule permits sponsors to select award judges. A finalist worries about favouritism. Keep the funding but complete one missing boundary: Sponsors may fund awards provided that _____.
rehearsal.sample: Sponsors may fund awards provided that an independent school panel selects the judges.

image.alt: A theater advertisement sits beside a positive theater review, then moves onto a separate page while the review stays the same.
image.caption: Moving the ad changes the layout, not the review. Separation can address a concern about influence; it does not prove independence by itself. AI-generated teaching illustration.

stages.title: Choose a workable boundary
stages.explanation: “Be fair” is a worthy wish and a difficult instruction for tomorrow’s editor. Try a boundary someone can apply: keep the sponsor out of selecting award winners. A qualification changes who, where, or under what conditions. Explain which concern your boundary answers and which benefit it preserves; a boundary reduces a risk rather than magically removing every doubt.
modelRows: Proposal
“Let sponsors announce upcoming shows.”
Objection
Readers may mistake a paid announcement for the editors’ pick.
One condition
“Run announcements only with a Paid advertisement label above the headline.” Where the label goes matters because readers encounter it before the pitch.
stages.model:
Proposal — “Let sponsors announce upcoming shows.”
Objection — Readers may mistake a paid announcement for the editors’ pick.
One condition — “Run announcements only with a Paid advertisement label above the headline.” Where the label goes matters because readers encounter it before the pitch.

questions.prompt: A sponsor wants a quote from a critic inside its ad. Which restriction addresses misleading excerpts?
options: Make ads shorter.
Require quoted words to preserve the critic’s judgment in context.
answers: Require quoted words to preserve the critic’s judgment in context.
questions.hint: Ask what a selective quotation might hide.
questions.explanation: A negative review can look positive when a phrase is lifted out of context.

alternate.prompt: Students worry a sponsor logo looks like the paper’s signature. Which rule targets that concern?
options: Keep sponsor logos out of the masthead.
Use fewer photographs.
answers: Keep sponsor logos out of the masthead.

rehearsal.prompt: The paper allows all businesses to sponsor awards. A finalist worries that a sponsor might also judge the competition. Add one condition to the policy.
rehearsal.sample: Accept award funding only if the sponsor has no role in selecting the winner.

questions.prompt: Which revision gives editors an enforceable rule?
options: Respect independence whenever possible.
Reject contracts that give advertisers a vote on story selection.
answers: Reject contracts that give advertisers a vote on story selection.
questions.hint: Could two editors apply the rule to the same contract?
questions.explanation: A voting right can be checked in the terms.

alternate.prompt: Which revision gives designers a usable boundary?
options: Put the sponsor credit below the byline in a box marked Sponsor.
Keep funding tasteful.
answers: Put the sponsor credit below the byline in a box marked Sponsor.

final.title: Set a policy for sponsored profiles
final.source:
Fictional newsroom file
Draft rule: “Accept a sponsor for any student-artist profile.” A drama student says the money could pay for portraits of backstage crews. A photographer objects that a costume shop wants the right to nominate every featured artist.
final.prompt: Write a revised policy and explain it in 3–5 sentences. Represent the strongest objection fairly, identify precisely what changes, and explain how your rule weighs the benefit of funding against the power to nominate.
rubric: Objection: Accurately represents a concern about selection power.
Qualification: Writes a specific actionable policy boundary that responds to the objection.
Reasoning: Explains the effect of the boundary and weighs the benefit of portraits; accept different defensible policies.
final.delayedCheck: Next class, a club accepts donated sports equipment, but the donor wants to choose the captain. Write one condition that addresses the objection while considering the benefit.

title: Advertising 3 · Same decision, different reader
objective: Explain how an argument addresses a reader’s needs and defend one decision to two audiences (AP Lang 1.B, 2.B).

stages.title: Hear the reader’s question
stages.explanation: One newspaper decision, two worried readers. A subscriber asks who chose the stories. A performer wants to know whether their play can appear. Sending both “Everything is fine!” is admirably efficient at answering neither. Keep the facts steady, but lead with the detail this person needs. Here, a labeled ad funds two arts pages; the editor still chooses the stories.
modelRows: A subscriber asks, “Who chose the story?”
“Our editors chose every story on these pages.” Chose answers the question about independence.
A performer asks, “Will our play be covered?”
“The ad buys space for two more arts pages.” Space explains what funding makes possible without promising any group a review.
stages.model:
A subscriber asks, “Who chose the story?” — “Our editors chose every story on these pages.” Chose answers the question about independence.
A performer asks, “Will our play be covered?” — “The ad buys space for two more arts pages.” Space explains what funding makes possible without promising any group a review.

questions.prompt: “Will paying buy a positive review?” Which fact should the editor lead with?
options: Two pages will be added.
Only student editors choose and evaluate shows.
answers: Only student editors choose and evaluate shows.
questions.hint: What power is this reader worried about?
questions.explanation: The question concerns who controls judgment.

alternate.prompt: A reader asks whether the paper recommends the advertised café. Which opening addresses that question?
options: The café bought the space for its own message.
The café paid on time.
answers: The café bought the space for its own message.

questions.prompt: A stage manager asks how a backstage crew can be considered for coverage. Which opening fits?
options: Our contract lasts a month.
Crews can send pitches directly to the arts editor.
answers: Crews can send pitches directly to the arts editor.
questions.hint: What action does the stage manager want to take?
questions.explanation: The submission route gives the crew an actionable answer.

alternate.prompt: The treasurer asks how the next issue will be printed. Which detail belongs first?
options: The ad payment covers this issue’s printing invoice.
Reviews have student bylines.
answers: The ad payment covers this issue’s printing invoice.

rehearsal.prompt: Shared facts: a labeled ad funds a festival insert; student editors select reviews. A subscriber asks whether the advertiser chooses the verdict. Complete just the explanation: Student editors choose the reviews, so _____.
rehearsal.sample: Student editors choose the reviews, so paying for the insert does not give the advertiser control of the verdict.

image.alt: Two readers look at the same exhibition paper; one focuses on who selects the art, the other on submitting a photo before a deadline.
image.caption: Both readers get the same facts. The opening detail changes because one needs to know who chooses and the other needs to know how to submit. AI-generated teaching illustration.

stages.title: Change the opening reason
stages.explanation: Changing the reader does not give you permission to change reality. Think of two lamps lighting different parts of the same desk. One reader needs the selection rule; another needs a submission route. Lead with the relevant fact, then explain why it answers that reader’s question. You are changing emphasis, not inventing a better deal.
modelRows: Shared facts
The paper will print a separately labeled festival insert. Vendors buy listings; students write reviews.
To a reader
“Look for the listing label when planning your visit: vendors describe themselves there. Student reviewers sign their own assessments.”
To a vendor
“A listing gives visitors your booth details. Buying one reserves space for those details while reviewers make their own selections.”
stages.model:
Shared facts — The paper will print a separately labeled festival insert. Vendors buy listings; students write reviews.
To a reader — “Look for the listing label when planning your visit: vendors describe themselves there. Student reviewers sign their own assessments.”
To a vendor — “A listing gives visitors your booth details. Buying one reserves space for those details while reviewers make their own selections.”

questions.prompt: Which change most directly adapts the reader’s opening for vendors?
options: Use “Dear valued vendor.”
Explain what a paid listing lets a booth owner tell visitors.
answers: Explain what a paid listing lets a booth owner tell visitors.
questions.hint: What does a vendor need to decide?
questions.explanation: Knowing what space buys helps a vendor decide whether to participate.

alternate.prompt: Adapt a note for families asking how to identify paid content. Which detail should lead?
options: Thank them warmly.
Tell them where the paid label appears.
answers: Tell them where the paid label appears.

rehearsal.prompt: A student critic asks how the festival insert affects their review. Write an opening using the shared facts above.
rehearsal.sample: You still choose the judgment you sign your name to. The vendor’s paid listing has its own label.

questions.prompt: Which pitch keeps the facts accurate while appealing to a vendor?
options: Paying secures a favorable review.
Your listing can help visitors find your booth.
answers: Your listing can help visitors find your booth.
questions.hint: Compare each promise with what the vendor buys.
questions.explanation: A listing can supply directions. A review is a separate editorial decision.

alternate.prompt: A photographer asks what a sponsor-funded travel allowance guarantees. The editor still selects photos. Which pitch is accurate?
options: Your trip can be funded even if no photo is selected.
Your photo is guaranteed a page.
answers: Your trip can be funded even if no photo is selected.

final.title: Write two notes about one decision
final.source:
Fictional newsroom file
The paper will accept a framing shop’s ad to pay for a photo spread of the student exhibition. The art editor alone selects six works. All exhibitors may submit one photo by Friday. The ad will be labeled and printed on the back page.
final.prompt: Write two brief notes of two sentences each. A subscriber asks whether the shop chooses the art. An exhibitor asks how to get their work considered. Explain the decision to each using the same newsroom facts. Add one sentence explaining why you led with different details.
rubric: Subscriber: Addresses selection or independence with an accurate fact and explains its significance.
Exhibitor: Gives accurate actionable information about consideration without guaranteeing selection.
Audience reasoning: Explains why the two readers need different opening details while maintaining the same policy.
final.delayedCheck: Next class, a club has one free room with ten seats and sign-up closes Friday. Write two openings: one for someone asking about cost, another for someone asking how to join. Keep the facts fixed.

title: Ethics 1 · Does My Reason Support My Decision?
objective: Identify a leap in reasoning and defend a decision with evidence and a limit (4a.1, 4b.1).

stages.title: Spot the leap
stages.explanation: The team wins after one early practice. By lunchtime, someone wants dawn sessions forever. Apparently the sun has joined the coaching staff. The win is real; its cause is still a question. Separate what happened from what supposedly caused it. A reason supports a decision only when you can explain the connection, including what the evidence leaves uncertain.
modelRows: Observation
We held one early practice and then won one game. Both events happened.
Leap
“Early practice made us win.” The result alone cannot separate practice time from the opponent, the lineup, or luck.
Decision
Try two more sessions before requiring everyone to attend. A trial lets us gather evidence at a smaller cost.
stages.model:
Observation — We held one early practice and then won one game. Both events happened.
Leap — “Early practice made us win.” The result alone cannot separate practice time from the opponent, the lineup, or luck.
Decision — Try two more sessions before requiring everyone to attend. A trial lets us gather evidence at a smaller cost.

questions.prompt: Which statement reports an observation?
options: Early sessions guarantee wins.
We won the match after Tuesday’s early practice.
The opponent lost because we trained early.
answers: We won the match after Tuesday’s early practice.
questions.hint: Which could a calendar and score sheet verify?
questions.explanation: The timing and score are recorded. The cause still needs investigation.

alternate.prompt: A club switched rooms before a busy meeting. Which fact is directly observed?
options: More students attended that meeting.
The new room attracted everyone.
answers: More students attended that meeting.

questions.prompt: “We won once, so every team should train early.” What is the leap?
options: It generalizes from one team and one match.
It uses a comparison across many teams.
It describes a scheduling conflict.
answers: It generalizes from one team and one match.
questions.hint: How many cases support the word every?
questions.explanation: One success gives little basis for a rule covering other teams.

alternate.prompt: One student liked a workshop, so the organizer says all grades need it. What is the problem?
options: A workshop cannot be evaluated.
One response is being extended to every grade.
answers: One response is being extended to every grade.

rehearsal.prompt: A club moved its meeting and attendance rose once. Complete just the missing limit: More students came, but we cannot yet conclude _____.
rehearsal.sample: More students came, but we cannot yet conclude that the room caused the increase; the meeting topic might also have attracted people.

image.alt: An athlete connects sunrise practice with a trophy, then compares practice records while considering weather and opponents.
image.caption: The arrow from practice to trophy is the athlete’s claim. Comparable records and alternative explanations are needed to test it. AI-generated teaching illustration.

stages.title: Calibrate the decision
stages.explanation: One good result can earn a second look without earning a permanent rule. Compare similar situations, explain why the difference matters, and say what could change your mind. In the fictional log below, the opponent stays the same, but two games still leave other explanations. A trial is a way to learn, not a promise that your first guess will win.
modelRows: Fictional log
Against the same opponent, the team made 6 passing errors after an early session and 10 after an afternoon one.
Reason
Fewer errors matter if accurate passing is the goal.
Limit
Two games leave room for other explanations. Compare more games and ask who can attend before setting a rule.
stages.model:
Fictional log — Against the same opponent, the team made 6 passing errors after an early session and 10 after an afternoon one.
Reason — Fewer errors matter if accurate passing is the goal.
Limit — Two games leave room for other explanations. Compare more games and ask who can attend before setting a rule.

questions.prompt: Which comparison would better test whether timing helps passing?
options: Early practice against beginners versus late practice against champions.
Run the same passing drill with the same players at both times.
answers: Run the same passing drill with the same players at both times.
questions.hint: Hold the task and players steady.
questions.explanation: A comparable drill reduces differences unrelated to time.

alternate.prompt: Which comparison better tests two meeting formats?
options: The same group doing similar tasks in each format.
Two clubs with unrelated goals.
answers: The same group doing similar tasks in each format.

rehearsal.prompt: The captain proposes a trial after one drill with fewer missed passes. The limit is supplied: one drill cannot justify a permanent rule. Supply just the reason that supports trying again.
rehearsal.sample: Fewer missed passes suggest the session may help accuracy, so another comparable drill could test whether that pattern continues.

questions.prompt: One player cannot get an early bus. Which recommendation weighs that fact?
options: Count absence as lack of effort.
Test a session everyone can reach before making attendance compulsory.
answers: Test a session everyone can reach before making attendance compulsory.
questions.hint: Who would bear the cost of the proposed rule?
questions.explanation: Access changes whether the policy is fair even if practice helps.

alternate.prompt: A useful evening tutorial overlaps the last bus. Which response fits?
options: Require everyone to stay.
Try an accessible slot and check participation.
answers: Try an accessible slot and check participation.

final.title: Advise the debate captain
final.source: Fictional log: In two rounds without a warm-up, speakers went over time 4 and 3 times. In two rounds with a ten-minute warm-up, they went over 1 and 2 times. Both warm-up rounds used familiar topics. Two bus riders cannot arrive early.
final.prompt: Should the club require an early warm-up? Write 3–5 sentences. Use the log, explain why the pattern matters, and say how the uncertainty or access issue affects your decision.
rubric: Decision: Gives a defensible recommendation, including a trial or an alternative.
Reason: Accurately uses a comparison and connects it to timekeeping.
Limit: Weighs a plausible alternative explanation or access constraint without claiming the warm-up alone caused the change.
final.delayedCheck: Next class, a fictional class gets higher quiz scores after changing seats once. Name the observation, give another possible explanation, and propose a cautious next step.

title: Ethics 2 · Compare Two Good Options
objective: Identify a community need and compare feasible responses against the same criteria (3a.3, 3b.3).

stages.title: Hear the need
stages.explanation: Your club arrives at the library with donated books and excellent intentions. The shelves are full. A child is waiting for someone to read with. You have solved the problem of not having enough boxes. Unfortunately, that was not the library’s problem. Ask the people who will use the project what they need, then turn their answer into a result you can check.
modelRows: First offer
“We can donate books.” This names what the club can give.
Partner’s words
“Our shelves are full. Children need someone to read with.” The unmet need is company and help during reading hour.
Criterion
Ask how many children can read with someone on Saturday. That measure follows the request.
stages.model:
First offer — “We can donate books.” This names what the club can give.
Partner’s words — “Our shelves are full. Children need someone to read with.” The unmet need is company and help during reading hour.
Criterion — Ask how many children can read with someone on Saturday. That measure follows the request.

questions.prompt: Which question best clarifies the request?
options: What color should our donation boxes be?
How many reading partners do you need and when?
answers: How many reading partners do you need and when?
questions.hint: Ask what would change for children.
questions.explanation: The answer tells the club how to staff the hour.

alternate.prompt: A garden needs help watering in July. What should volunteers clarify?
options: Which days lack watering coverage?
What slogan should go on the gate?
answers: Which days lack watering coverage?

questions.prompt: Which observation shows the library need was met?
options: Many boxes arrived.
A photo was published.
Children who requested partners had someone to read with.
answers: Children who requested partners had someone to read with.
questions.hint: Look for the result named by the partner.
questions.explanation: A count of reading partnerships tests the actual goal.

alternate.prompt: A pantry asks for clear shelf labels. Which result matters most?
options: Many signs were printed.
Visitors could find the items they needed.
answers: Visitors could find the items they needed.

rehearsal.prompt: A garden asks for watering help on uncovered weekdays. Complete one missing success measure: We should count _____ rather than volunteer photos.
rehearsal.sample: We should count previously uncovered weekdays that now have a reliable waterer, rather than volunteer photos.

image.alt: A volunteer brings books to full library shelves while a child waits by an empty chair; later the volunteer sits and reads with the child.
image.caption: The empty partner’s chair identifies the unmet need. Count reading partnerships, not donated boxes. AI-generated teaching illustration.

stages.title: Compare on common ground
stages.explanation: Two plans can both help and still help differently. Compare them using the same question: how many children get a partner, or how long can each pair read? Do not praise one plan for reach and the other for cheerful posters. Then name the trade-off: what worthwhile thing does your chosen plan give up? The partner’s priorities decide which cost matters most.
modelRows: Library options
Four volunteers can each read with one child for the full hour, or each can run two half-hour sessions.
Reach
Full sessions serve four children; split sessions serve eight. The comparison uses the same hour and volunteers.
Trade-off
Split sessions increase access but halve the time each child has to finish a story.
stages.model:
Library options — Four volunteers can each read with one child for the full hour, or each can run two half-hour sessions.
Reach — Full sessions serve four children; split sessions serve eight. The comparison uses the same hour and volunteers.
Trade-off — Split sessions increase access but halve the time each child has to finish a story.

questions.prompt: Which comparison uses one measure for both plans?
options: A has cheerful posters; B costs little.
A covers four shifts; B covers two shifts.
answers: A covers four shifts; B covers two shifts.
questions.hint: Finish the same question for each plan.
questions.explanation: Counting covered shifts lets the partner compare coverage directly.

alternate.prompt: Which comparison measures accessibility for both sites?
options: Count the steps at each entrance.
Compare one site’s price with the other’s size.
answers: Count the steps at each entrance.

rehearsal.prompt: A club can offer three 60-minute tutoring sessions or six 30-minute sessions. A learner needs uninterrupted time. The shared measure is minutes per session. Complete only the missing comparison: The first plan gives each learner _____ compared with the second.
rehearsal.sample: The first plan gives each learner 60 uninterrupted minutes rather than 30, so there is more time to finish one difficult problem.

questions.prompt: Which sentence names a cost of the chosen plan?
options: Both ideas are great.
Short sessions include more readers but leave less time for longer stories.
answers: Short sessions include more readers but leave less time for longer stories.
questions.hint: Name something the other option offers.
questions.explanation: A trade-off states what is lost as well as gained.

alternate.prompt: Which sentence gives a trade-off for rotating volunteers?
options: More people can help, but children see a different partner.
Rotation is the best system.
answers: More people can help, but children see a different partner.

final.title: Recommend a welcome plan
final.source: Fictional partner note: “Twelve new students need help finding classrooms on Monday. Four have asked for someone to walk with them. We have two guides and 40 minutes. A group tour takes 20 minutes; a personal walk takes 10 minutes per guide. A map is available.”
final.prompt: Propose two workable uses of the guides. Compare both against the same need, recommend one, and name a cost or unmet need you would check with the students. Write 3–5 sentences.
rubric: Options: Offers two distinguishable, feasible responses using the available people and time.
Comparison: Evaluates both against a shared need from the note.
Choice: Justifies a recommendation and acknowledges a concrete trade-off.
final.delayedCheck: Next class, a pantry can offer one long collection window or two shorter windows with the same staffing hours. Name a need, compare both plans against it, and state one trade-off.

title: Ethics 3 · What Would the Other Person Say?
objective: Explain another person’s belief in terms they could recognize, then explain what informs your own judgment (1b.1, 1b.2).

stages.title: Represent the reason
stages.explanation: The baton hits the track. The coach thinks about the reserve runner waiting for a chance. The runner thinks about the hand signal changed yesterday. It is tempting to summarize an opponent as “a person who enjoys being wrong.” Convenient; rarely accurate. Use their actual words to explain what matters to them. Both people may value fairness while disagreeing about what fairness requires here.
modelRows: Coach
“I saw the baton hit the ground. We owe the reserve runner a fair trial.” The coach values an open selection process.
Runner
“We changed our hand signal yesterday. Give us one practice with it.” The runner values a fair chance to learn the change.
Fair account
Both care about fairness. They disagree about what evidence should count in this decision.
stages.model:
Coach — “I saw the baton hit the ground. We owe the reserve runner a fair trial.” The coach values an open selection process.
Runner — “We changed our hand signal yesterday. Give us one practice with it.” The runner values a fair chance to learn the change.
Fair account — Both care about fairness. They disagree about what evidence should count in this decision.

questions.prompt: Which summary would the runner recognize?
options: I should never be replaced.
I want time to practice the changed signal before selection.
The coach dislikes me.
answers: I want time to practice the changed signal before selection.
questions.hint: Use the reason the runner actually gave.
questions.explanation: The runner challenges the timing of the decision.

alternate.prompt: “Let applicants use paper because some lack internet.” Which summary is fair?
options: Reject all technology.
Keep an accessible route to apply.
answers: Keep an accessible route to apply.

questions.prompt: Which reply checks an interpretation?
options: You just want special treatment.
Would another practice give you a fair test of the new signal?
answers: Would another practice give you a fair test of the new signal?
questions.hint: Ask a question the person can correct.
questions.explanation: The runner can confirm or refine that reading.

alternate.prompt: A teammate asks to rotate captains. Which reply checks their reason?
options: You dislike our captain.
Are you hoping more players can learn the role?
answers: Are you hoping more players can learn the role?

rehearsal.prompt: A teammate says, “Rotate captains so everyone can learn to lead.” Keep the proposal fixed and supply the missing reason: They want rotating captains because _____.
rehearsal.sample: They want rotating captains because the role gives more teammates a chance to practise leadership, not just to watch it.

image.alt: Beside a dropped baton, two people imagine different concerns: giving a reserve a chance and practising a changed hand signal.
image.caption: The imagined insets illustrate the reasons given in the model. They are not evidence of private thoughts; check your account against what each person says. AI-generated teaching illustration.

stages.title: Locate your own view
stages.explanation: Once you can explain their reason fairly, locate your own. “I disagree” gives us your destination; now show one step of the journey. An example, commitment, or class discussion can explain why you choose a rule. You need not share anything private. You can take a concern seriously and still judge that another concern carries more weight.
modelRows: Different proposal
A director wants an experienced soloist because rehearsal time is short. A newcomer asks for an open audition.
Own position
I would hold a short audition.
Influence
A rehearsal where a substitute learned quickly taught me that an unfamiliar voice can be ready. I still understand the director’s worry about time.
stages.model:
Different proposal — A director wants an experienced soloist because rehearsal time is short. A newcomer asks for an open audition.
Own position — I would hold a short audition.
Influence — A rehearsal where a substitute learned quickly taught me that an unfamiliar voice can be ready. I still understand the director’s worry about time.

questions.prompt: Which sentence explains an influence on a judgment?
options: I just know auditions are fair.
Seeing a substitute learn in one rehearsal made me willing to try an audition.
answers: Seeing a substitute learn in one rehearsal made me willing to try an audition.
questions.hint: Look for a connection between an experience and a belief.
questions.explanation: The experience explains why the speaker values an opportunity to demonstrate readiness.

alternate.prompt: Which writer connects a commitment to a decision?
options: Everyone knows the answer.
Because I value keeping promises, I would honor the earlier booking.
answers: Because I value keeping promises, I would honor the earlier booking.

rehearsal.prompt: A musician wants blind auditions because names may influence judges. Their reason is supplied: anonymity could keep attention on the performance. State your own judgment and one public example or commitment that informs it.
rehearsal.sample: I favour blind auditions because I value giving unfamiliar performers a fair hearing. That commitment makes me want judges to hear the performance before seeing a familiar name.

questions.prompt: Which disagreement takes the director seriously?
options: The director fears all new singers.
A short audition costs rehearsal time, but it can reveal a prepared newcomer.
answers: A short audition costs rehearsal time, but it can reveal a prepared newcomer.
questions.hint: Keep the concern recognizable.
questions.explanation: The response names the time cost and explains a reason to accept it.

alternate.prompt: Which answer fairly challenges a request for anonymous voting?
options: The requester is secretive.
Privacy can protect honest votes, though I also want a public count.
answers: Privacy can protect honest votes, though I also want a public count.

final.title: Write both sides of the selection meeting
final.source: Fictional council notes: Lin says, “Give the festival stall to last year’s group. We promised they could return if they cleaned up, and they did.” Sam says, “Open a draw. Four new groups have never had a chance to take part.”
final.prompt: Write 4–5 sentences. Give the strongest fair account of the view you are less inclined to choose, state your own rule, and explain one experience, example or commitment that informs it. You may propose a third rule.
rubric: Fair account: Reconstructs a competing view using its actual reason without inventing motives.
Judgment: States a clear rule and explains what it values in this case.
Influence: Connects an example, experience or commitment to the judgment; private disclosure is unnecessary.
final.delayedCheck: Next class, a fictional club member says, “Keep one quiet table so people can finish work.” Give a fair account of that reason, then explain your own rule and one commitment behind it.

title: Ethics 4 · Turn an Apology into a Repair
objective: Take responsibility for a choice and devise a repair plan the affected person can evaluate (A4 1.c, A3 1.c).

stages.title: Name the impact
stages.explanation: You tear the only concert poster while moving a display. The organizer stares at the missing time. “Sorry if the poster felt torn” will not help; paper has no useful opinion on the matter. Own the action you controlled and name what it cost someone else. “I tore the poster, so visitors cannot see the time” gives you an actual problem to repair.
modelRows: Vague
“Sorry about the poster.” The organizer cannot tell whether you know what went wrong.
Accountable
“I tore the only concert poster while moving our display. People walking by can no longer see the time.”
First question
“Is this still the best place to reach tonight’s audience?” The organizer can help define a repair.
stages.model:
Vague — “Sorry about the poster.” The organizer cannot tell whether you know what went wrong.
Accountable — “I tore the only concert poster while moving our display. People walking by can no longer see the time.”
First question — “Is this still the best place to reach tonight’s audience?” The organizer can help define a repair.

questions.prompt: Which opening owns a decision?
options: Mistakes were made with the notice.
I took down your notice before the event ended.
Nobody told me to be careful.
answers: I took down your notice before the event ended.
questions.hint: Find who did what.
questions.explanation: Naming the action makes it possible to address the consequence.

alternate.prompt: Which opening owns a roster mistake?
options: I copied the old roster and left you off.
The roster got confusing.
answers: I copied the old roster and left you off.

questions.prompt: What is the most direct impact of posting the wrong room number?
options: The writer feels awkward.
Visitors may go to the wrong room.
answers: Visitors may go to the wrong room.
questions.hint: Whose next action would the mistake affect?
questions.explanation: The misleading direction creates a practical problem for visitors.

alternate.prompt: An organizer omits the sign-language interpreter from the booking. Which impact matters first?
options: The form looks untidy.
Some attendees may lose access to the talk.
answers: Some attendees may lose access to the talk.

rehearsal.prompt: You posted the wrong meeting room. The action is already named: “I put Room 12 instead of Room 21.” Supply only its likely impact.
rehearsal.sample: People following the notice may miss the start while looking for the meeting in the wrong room.

image.alt: A torn music poster remains damaged during a large empty apology bubble; in the last panel a replacement is checked with the organizer.
image.caption: The speech bubble does not repair the poster. The final panel adds a useful action and the organizer’s check. AI-generated teaching illustration.

stages.title: Make repair checkable
stages.explanation: A magnificent apology cannot tell visitors when the concert starts. A useful repair can. Choose an action within your authority, say who will do it and when, and let the affected person judge whether it works. Replacing something is not automatically restoring what they needed. Ask, check, and adjust; add one concrete safeguard against repeating the mistake.
modelRows: Loss
A club’s mislabeled file left a designer out of the printed credits.
Repair
The editor offers a corrected online credit today and a correction in the next print issue.
Check
The editor sends the proposed credit to the designer before publication and checks the printed copy afterward.
stages.model:
Loss — A club’s mislabeled file left a designer out of the printed credits.
Repair — The editor offers a corrected online credit today and a correction in the next print issue.
Check — The editor sends the proposed credit to the designer before publication and checks the printed copy afterward.

questions.prompt: Which step lets the affected person judge the repair?
options: Promise to do better.
Send the corrected credit for the designer to review.
answers: Send the corrected credit for the designer to review.
questions.hint: Who can confirm whether the correction is accurate?
questions.explanation: The designer can catch another error before it appears in print.

alternate.prompt: A group replaces a borrowed cable. Which check matters?
options: Ask the owner to test it with their device.
Count how many people heard the apology.
answers: Ask the owner to test it with their device.

rehearsal.prompt: You accidentally canceled a room booking. A comparable room is available. Write the missing check after you reserve it.
rehearsal.sample: I’ll show the new room and time to the organizer today and ask whether the space works for their group.

questions.prompt: Which plan prevents a repeat?
options: Everyone should be careful.
The editor checks each credit against the signed contributor list before printing.
answers: The editor checks each credit against the signed contributor list before printing.
questions.hint: Find a person, a check and a time.
questions.explanation: The rule gives someone a specific action before the harm can recur.

alternate.prompt: Which plan prevents another missed pickup?
options: Try harder next week.
The trip leader confirms pickup time with the driver before sending the notice.
answers: The trip leader confirms pickup time with the driver before sending the notice.

final.title: Respond to the students who missed the bus
final.source:
Fictional trip report: You sent the wrong departure time. Two students missed the museum visit and had already paid. The teacher handles refunds. The museum offers a second visit next Thursday, but you do not know if the students can attend.
Alternative fictional context: use a paid art workshop instead of the museum visit. The same wrong departure time, two missed students, teacher-controlled refunds and uncertain Thursday availability apply.
final.prompt: Choose the museum visit or art workshop context. Write the message you would send the students and one prevention step. Own the error, offer a repair within your authority, and give a time and way for the students to tell you whether it meets their needs.
rubric: Ownership: Identifies the writer’s action and a concrete impact.
Repair: Offers a feasible next action with a responsible person and time; does not promise an unauthorized refund.
Follow-up: Gives the students a meaningful say and identifies a specific prevention check.
final.delayedCheck: Next class, imagine you left a contributor out of a group credit. Write an accountable opening, a repair within your control, and a way for that contributor to check it.

title: Ethics 5 · Lead, Then Check the Effect
objective: Practice a leadership move, identify its observable effect, and choose an adjustment (3d.1, 3d.2).
